articles.title: Announcing Welch Summer School 2026
articles.preview: A remarkable opportunity for high school students and freshmen to engage in hands-on crystallization research this summer.

body.full_title: Welch Summer School 2026: Hands-on Research Experience
body.lead_text: The Welch Center for Advanced Bioactive Materials Crystallization is pleased to announce the Welch Summer School 2026. This initiative offers a remarkable opportunity for high school students and freshmen who are passionate about science, technology, and research.

content_blocks.content: Participants will engage in scientific research focused on crystallization and its applications within pharmaceuticals, energy, and agriculture. They will have the opportunity to work in the laboratories of the center's seven faculty members from three different departments, benefiting from the guidance and mentorship of over 30 postdoctoral fellows and Ph.D. students.

The program is scheduled to run from June to August 2026, with flexible start and end dates to accommodate participants' schedules. To ensure students can fully engage with the work, applicants should have at least one year of chemistry experience. Each participant is typically paired with a postdoc or a PhD student who acts as a daily mentor, assisting with experimental training, project guidance, and helping them integrate into the lab environment.
We regularly collaborate with faculty across the college to organize lectures and activities aimed at introducing students to STEM research, academic pathways, and related career options.

We are proud of the positive impact our previous summer schools have had. Last year, 11 high school students and freshmen from various schools and universities around Houston gained invaluable hands-on experience in our state-of-the-art laboratories. This year, we anticipate admitting an even larger cohort of enthusiastic learners.
If you have any questions or need further information, please don't hesitate to reach out to smhatre@central.uh.edu.

articles.title: Nurturing Innovation: Summer Students 2025
articles.preview: Eleven dedicated high school and university freshman students embarked on an exciting journey, preparing for future endeavors in scientific research.

body.full_title: Nurturing Innovation: Summer Students Develop Research Skills and Futures at the Welch Center
body.image_caption: The 2025 cohort of summer researchers at the Durga D. and Sushila Agrawal Engineering Research Building
body.lead_text: Eleven dedicated high school and university freshman students are embarking on an exciting journey, preparing for future endeavors in scientific research and industry.

content_blocks.content: At this pivotal moment in their careers, they are being mentored by experienced researchers at the Welch Center for Advanced Bioactive Materials Crystallization, immersing themselves in a variety of inspiring research themes. The center's researchers are not only spearheading innovations but also cultivating the next generation to confront the challenges of the dynamic field of crystallization, crucial for advancements in healthcare, energy, and environmental sustainability.

These students are engaged in meaningful research that has the potential to benefit humanity. Among them, Kayla Nguyen, a freshman, and Sarah Morrison, a junior in Chemical Engineering at the University of Houston, are making significant strides. Kayla's exploration of evaporation methods in pyrazinamide crystallization, a vital treatment in the fight against tuberculosis, exemplifies the impact of this work. Sarah, alongside freshman Imad Shaikh from the University of Texas at San Antonio, is investigating the crystallization and growth patterns of cholesterol in blood vessels, seeking ways to manage its development.

Sravya Dutta, an incoming junior in Cell and Molecular Biology at Baylor University, is delving into biocrystallization studies under the mentorship of senior researchers, laying a solid foundation for her future career. High school students Krithika Srinivas, Mahika Shah, and Sanjita Chinta are witnessing firsthand the transformative nature of scientific research and its application for the betterment of society.

Beyond bioactive materials, several students are channeling their efforts into optimizing catalysts for energy extraction. Kaiden Stassen, a freshman at UH, is developing methods to create bifunctional zeolite catalysts, employed in the oil and petrochemical industries. Raquel Nwosu from the University of Texas at Arlington is enhancing the catalyst effectiveness by modifying microstructures. Penda Diop (Houston Community College) and Annabelle Choi (Carnegie Vanguard High School) are also exploring ways to amplify the catalytic activity of zeolites through innovative functionalization and structural transformation.

content_blocks.title: 2025 Summer Student Cohort
content_blocks.description: Meet the eleven students driving innovation.

content_blocks.content: The guidance from the center's experts, paired with access to state-of-the-art facilities, is shaping a bright future for the biomedical and energy sectors in Texas and across the nation. The invaluable experiences that these students are accumulating at the center are nurturing the seeds of innovation and creativity, laying the foundation for a transformative future that holds great potential.

articles.title: Prof. Burcham Elected to National Academy of Engineering
articles.preview: Prof. Christopher Burcham, a distinguished member of our Industrial Advisory Board, has been elected to the prestigious National Academy of Engineering.

body.full_title: Congratulations! Prof. Burcham Elected to the National Academy of Engineering
body.image_caption: Prof. Christopher Burcham, NAE Class of 2026
body.lead_text: Prof. Christopher Burcham, a distinguished member of our Industrial Advisory Board, has been elected to the prestigious National Academy of Engineering (NAE).

content_blocks.content: This distinguished recognition underscores his pioneering contributions in the areas of crystallization, particle engineering, and process control. Through his innovative research and its practical applications, Prof. Burcham has significantly advanced pharmaceutical engineering, leading to the development and market introduction of new and effective therapies.

This year, Prof. Burcham is among the 130 exceptional individuals from the United States elected to the academy and is included within a total of 2,534 members who possess the highest professional distinctions in the engineering discipline. Membership in the academy is reserved for those who have made extraordinary contributions to engineering research, practice, or education.
We extend our warmest congratulations to Prof. Burcham on this well-deserved honor.

articles.title: Inaugural Welch Crystallization Symposium
articles.preview: The inaugural biennial symposium brought together nearly 100 participants from industry and academia to discuss nucleation, polymorphism, and crystal growth.

body.full_title: Welch Crystallization Symposium: Fostering Collaboration and Advancing Chemistry
body.image_caption: The inaugural biennial Welch Crystallization Symposium.
body.lead_text: The inaugural biennial Welch Crystallization Symposium was conducted on September 5, 2025, at the Agrawal Engineering Research Building of the University of Houston (UH). This full-day event drew nearly 100 participants from the pharmaceutical industry nationwide, as well as representatives from academia.

content_blocks.content: The program commenced with opening remarks delivered by Dr. Adam Kuspa, President of the Welch Foundation, and Prof. Jeffrey Rimer, Program Director of the Welch Center for Advanced Bioactive Materials Crystallization at UH. Dr. Kuspa emphasized the Foundation's significant contributions to advancing chemistry in Texas through single-investigator research grants, departmental programs, endowed chairs, and other specialized initiatives. The Foundation’s Catalyst for Discovery Program Grants, which also support the Welch Center for Advanced Bioactive Materials Crystallization at UH, aim to foster collaboration by funding research teams across the state addressing critical challenges at the forefront of chemistry.
Industry Perspectives & Keynote Speakers

The symposium facilitated a vigorous exchange of knowledge concerning crystallization, focusing on nucleation, polymorphism, and crystal growth. The agenda featured two plenary sessions and four keynote presentations by senior scientists from leading American pharmaceutical companies.

content_blocks.title: Plenary & Keynote Highlights
items: Dr. Christopher Burcham (Eli Lilly) discussed the advantages and challenges associated with continuous crystallization within the pharmaceutical sector.
Dr. Kevin Girard (Pfizer) elaborated on advancements in continuous crystallization, isolation, and drying capabilities at Pfizer.

Dr. Christopher Marton (Bristol Myers Squibb) recent developments in high-throughput polymorph screening and crystallization techniques from the Materials Engineering and Crystallization group at Bristol Myers Squibb.
Dr. Manish Kelkar (AbbVie) examined emerging technologies in pharmaceutical crystallization, specifically highlighting AbbVie’s ongoing development efforts.

Dr. Megan Ketchum (GlaxoSmithKline)discussed semi-continuous crystallization, illustrating a case study involving active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) wherein both continuous and batch manufacturing methods were strategically applied to fulfill specific quality requirements.
Dr. Xiaolong Zhu (Merck) focused on polymorphism and the impact of molecular physical properties, demonstrating how such properties can influence the design of polymorphs.

items.caption: Dr. Christopher Burcham delivering a plenary address on continuous crystallization.
Principal Investigators and the Industrial Advisory Board members.
Q and A with Dr. T. Randall Lee and Dr. Peter G. Vekilov.
Poster competition winners: Radhika Menon, Arshia Nosrati, and Kosar Rahimi Nosrabadi.

content_blocks.content: Academic Insights & Student Research

Invited academic speakers included Professor Peter Vekilov and Dr. Gul Zerze from the UH Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering. Dr. Vekilov advocated for leveraging nonclassical mechanisms in nucleation, growth, and inhibition of hematin crystals as an effective strategy to suppress malaria parasites. Meanwhile, Dr. Zerze presented a multi-scale framework linking sequence-based classification of human transcription factor effector domains with the phase behavior and nucleation landscapes of their assemblies.

A poster session featured 33 graduate students who showcased their research findings and engaged with their peers and industry professionals. Three winners were announced at the conclusion of the event: Kosar Rahimi Nosrabadi (1st Place), Arshia Nosrati (2nd Place), and Radhika Menon (3rd Place).

The symposium was a significant success, achieving its primary objective of fostering collaboration between pharmaceutical professionals and academia, enabling participants to present their scientific discoveries, exchange ideas, and deliberate on future directions in pharmaceutical crystallization research and development.

articles.title: Welch Crystallization Symposium 2026 Brings Together Leading Experts in Crystal Engineering and Pharmaceutical Manufacturing

content_blocks.content: The Welch Center for Advanced Bioactive Materials Crystallization at the University of Houston hosted its annual Welch Crystallization Symposium on October 9, 2026, bringing together more than 100 scientists, professors, researchers, and industry professionals from universities, research institutions, and pharmaceutical companies across the United States. The one-day event highlighted the latest advances in crystallization science, crystal engineering, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and biomaterials research.

The symposium served as a premier forum for academic and industrial leaders to exchange ideas on the science and technology of crystallization, a field that plays a critical role in the development of pharmaceuticals, advanced materials, and biological systems. Through scientific presentations, poster sessions, and industry exhibitions, participants explored emerging challenges and opportunities in understanding and controlling crystal formation.

The event opened with remarks from Dr. Adam Kuspa, President of the Welch Foundation, who emphasized the Foundation's longstanding commitment to advancing chemical research. Founded in 1954 and based in Houston, the Welch Foundation is among the nation's largest private funding sources supporting basic chemical research.

In his remarks, Dr. Kuspa highlighted the Foundation's investments in single-investigator grants, departmental programs, endowed chairs, and special initiatives at educational institutions throughout Texas. He also discussed the Foundation's Catalyst for Discovery Program Grants, which are designed to accelerate collaborative, team-based research aimed at addressing significant challenges at the forefront of chemistry.

Following the opening presentation, Prof. Jeffrey D. Rimer, Director of the Welch Center and Abraham E. Dukler Endowed Chair of Chemical Engineering at the University of Houston, provided an overview of the Center's mission and accomplishments. Prof. Rimer highlighted major research advances achieved during the past three years and described ongoing collaborative efforts focused on understanding and controlling crystallization processes relevant to healthcare, materials science, and pharmaceutical manufacturing.
The symposium featured four sessions, including a poster session, with seven internationally recognized experts from academia and the pharmaceutical industry presenting cutting-edge research.

Prof. Rimer opened the scientific program with a keynote lecture titled "Breaking the Rules of Classical Crystallization: An Unconventional Guide to Crystal Engineering." His presentation explored both classical crystal growth pathways, involving the addition of ions and molecules, and nonclassical crystallization pathways in which metastable precursor particles directly participate in nucleation and crystal growth. Drawing examples from kidney stone formation, biomineralization, and pharmaceutical compounds, he demonstrated how a deeper understanding of crystal nucleation can lead to materials with enhanced properties.

Prof. Rimer also showcased collaborative research at the Welch Center focused on amorphous precursor assemblies, polymorph selection, and innovative methods for directing crystal growth through molecular modifiers, engineered surfaces, and coacervate systems.

Representing Eli Lilly and Company, Dr. Samir Kulkarni, Director of Engineering, presented "Turning Industrial Crystallization Data into Decisions: A Connected Workflow Approach." Dr. Kulkarni addressed the growing challenge of managing large volumes of process development data generated throughout crystallization workflows. He described how a "digital thread" strategy can connect experimental, analytical, and manufacturing information into a unified system, enabling faster decision-making, improved process understanding, and more efficient translation of laboratory findings to commercial production. Dr. Alpana Thorat, Principal Scientist at Pfizer Inc., presented "Crystallization Guided by Fundamentals: Spherical Crystallization of Avibactam Tomilopil (AVT)." Her talk focused on spherical agglomeration as an advanced crystallization strategy for a mesophase active pharmaceutical ingredient. Dr. Thorat described the successful progression of the process from late-stage development through large-scale manufacturing, including scale-up to approximately 300 kilograms. The study demonstrated how fundamental crystallization principles can support robust pharmaceutical process development and commercialization.

In a presentation titled "Complex Coacervates for Polymorphism Control in Molecular Crystallization," Prof. Alamgir Karim, Dow Chair and Welch Foundation Professor in the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering at the University of Houston, discussed how coacervates can serve as biomimetic environments for directing crystallization. Prof. Karim demonstrated that complex coacervate systems can selectively concentrate calcium and oxalate ions, enabling precise control over crystal size, morphology, and polymorphic form. The results suggest that coacervates may provide powerful new tools for controlling biomineralization processes and designing advanced functional materials.

Dr. John Maggioni, Associate Engineering Fellow at Takeda Development Center Americas, presented "In Silico First: Takeda's Journey Toward Autonomous Crystallization Development." Dr. Maggioni outlined Takeda's strategy for creating increasingly autonomous, model-driven crystallization workflows that integrate prior knowledge, automated experimentation, and predictive modeling. Using examples involving solubility measurements and recrystallization processes, he demonstrated how computational tools can accelerate decision-making while helping scientists identify hidden process variables and optimize crystal properties. A highlight of the symposium was the presentation by Dr. Monika Warzecha of Vertex Pharmaceuticals, who discussed "Navigating Polymorphic Complexity: Templated Desolvation Strategy for the Controlled Crystallization of Drug Substance." Her research examined a compound exhibiting more than 150 identified solid-state phases. Dr. Warzecha detailed how a carefully designed sequence of solvent-mediated transformations was required to obtain the desired crystal form selected for development. The work emphasized the critical roles of lattice templating, structural compatibility, and controlled dissolution pathways in achieving reliable crystallization outcomes for pharmaceutical products.

Closing the invited speaker program, Dr. Manish Kelkar, Senior Principal Research Scientist at AbbVie Inc., delivered an engaging presentation titled "Necessity is the Mother of Invention! ... OR ... Is it Curiosity?" Using a real-world pharmaceutical process development case study, Kelkar illustrated how asking purposeful "why" questions can uncover hidden assumptions, challenge conventional approaches, and inspire innovative solutions. His talk encouraged students and researchers to view scientific curiosity as a critical driver of engineering creativity, efficiency, and discovery.

An important component of the symposium was the poster session, which featured research presentations from 32 graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and scientists representing institutions across the country. A panel of six judges from the pharmaceutical industry evaluated the posters based on scientific quality, originality, and presentation effectiveness. Following a competitive review process, the symposium recognized three outstanding contributions. The first prize was awarded to M. Osman Khalid, the second to Alejandro C. Veliz, and the third prize to Hariharan Annadurai. The awards highlighted the exceptional research being conducted by emerging scientists in crystallization and related disciplines.

In addition to the scientific program, five leading instrument manufacturers participated as exhibitors, providing attendees with opportunities to explore state-of-the-art analytical technologies used in crystallization research and development. Participating companies included Rigaku, Anton Paar, Technobis, Malvern Panalytical and Mettler Toledo. Representatives demonstrated advanced instrumentation for crystal characterization, particle analysis, thermal analysis, process monitoring, and materials research, giving attendees insight into the latest technological developments supporting both academic and industrial crystallization studies.

Five world-leading manufacturers showcased their state-of-the-art instruments for crystal characterization.

content_blocks.content: The Welch Crystallization Symposium-2026 reinforced the Welch Center's role as a national hub for crystallization science by fostering collaboration among researchers from academia, industry, and government-funded research programs. Through discussions spanning fundamental crystal growth mechanisms, digital transformation, autonomous experimentation, pharmaceutical process development, and biomimetic materials, the symposium highlighted the growing impact of crystallization research on healthcare, manufacturing, and advanced materials design.

As crystallization science continues to play a central role in addressing challenges across multiple disciplines, the annual symposium remains an important platform for exchanging ideas, building partnerships, and inspiring the next generation of scientific innovation.
